extracted.intended_audience: general literate readers of The Spectator (early-18th-century readers interested in manners, satire, monuments, and social conduct)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance and evaluative principles about satire/lampoons, the behaviour of writers and readers, and the taste and inscription of public monuments and epitaphs as given in Spectator essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anonymous/secret attacks on reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Secret stabs to a man's reputation (anonymous lampoons and pasquinades) betray a base, ungenerous spirit and inflict wounds that are often incurable to the sufferer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such anonymous lampoons not only wound publicly but cause secret shame and long-lasting distress to individuals and families. The author should consider the harm done to the person attacked: 'An Injury is not to be measured by the Notions of him that gives, but of him that receives it.' Examples and consequences in the text: Aristophanes' ridicule of Socrates (which nevertheless affected him), Pasquinades in Rome (which led to severe reprisals), and Aretine's career show the power and danger of anonymous satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temper wit with virtue and humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit and ridicule should be tempered by virtue and humanity; wit without humanity becomes barbarous and inhuman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make virtue, merit, or praiseworthy qualities the object of buffoonry. Lampoons that expose private persons, innocent young women, heads of families, or sober and just men are pernicious. Writers should weigh the moral consequences of their raillery and avoid inflicting needless misery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer discretion over petulant cleverness
rubrics_metrics.description: Indiscreet, heedless humour (a 'petulant humour' in an author) is often more harmful than deliberate ill-nature because it sacrifices friends and acquaintances to levity or ambition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should avoid careless jokes made for distinction that inadvertently damage reputations. The essay warns against sacrificing friends' reputations for a display of raillery and counsels authors to exercise discretion and consider who they harm when attempting to be witty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to satire with civility where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: A generous, civil response to an author who has lampooned you can defuse resentment and sometimes reform the satirist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples given: Julius Caesar invited Catullus to supper and befriended him after the lampoon; Cardinal Mazarin treated Quillet with kindness, leading the poet to expunge offending passages and dedicate a later edition to him. These examples are presented as models of how temperate, magnanimous behaviour can convert enemies into friends and reduce ill effects of ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on punitive suppression of satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Harsh, punitive measures against satirists can be brutal and morally condemnable, and may produce notoriety rather than cure the vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts leniency with cruel punishment: a Pope offered money for disclosure of a Pasquinade author and when the author revealed himself his tongue and hands were mutilated. This demonstrates the danger and injustice of violent repression as a response to satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monuments and epitaphs should accurately reflect the deceased
rubrics_metrics.description: Funeral monuments and inscriptions ought to represent the true character and deeds of the person, not extravagant or misleading honours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid lavish, incongruous imagery (e.g., representing a plain, rugged admiral as a foppish beau). Inscriptions should celebrate the actual notable actions rather than merely describing the manner of death. The writer recommends that public monuments be submitted to learned and tasteful persons before execution, to ensure accuracy and propriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epitaph language must be accessible and appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Epitaphs written in obscure languages (e.g., Greek or Hebrew) or excessively modest/obscure forms fail their public function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inscriptions should be intelligible to those who view them; too many monuments merely record dates or use inaccessible language, which reduces their value as public memorials. The essay criticises epitaphs that are either exaggeratedly laudatory or so modest/learned as to be inscrutable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public monuments reflect national taste and should observe antiquity and politeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasteful design of monuments and inscriptions is a sign of a nation's politeness and learning; other nations (the Dutch, in the text) may show better taste than one's own country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The composition (figures, ornaments, rostral crowns, festoons) and inscriptions ought to suit the character of the commemorated person and the public good. The essay urges learned oversight of public memorials and contrasts English follies with more antique and tasteful Dutch monuments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hosts may set the terms of their private company
rubrics_metrics.description: A host (or regular tavern humourist) has a right to control the conversation in his chosen company and to expect to be the principal speaker; intruders who habitually join uninvited are a nuisance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the letter from a bachelor who dines nightly at a tavern, the writer asserts his right to be the main speaker and to scold intruders: being constant to an hour and paying does not entitle strangers to displace the host's convivial role. Hosts may therefore enforce rules of conduct in their own gatherings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social visiting etiquette: distance and reserved acquaintance can be politeness
rubrics_metrics.description: For certain acquaintances (notably women of limited conversational capacity), the best form of politeness is distance and silence rather than intimate visits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The example letter advising a woman to 'pay visits, but never see one another' advocates formal civility without personal intimacy: maintain appearances and civil forms but avoid deeper acquaintance with those who add nothing to conversation. For some social relationships, reserved politeness preserves good breeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: On health and regimen: avoid over-anxiety and over-management of life
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive attention to bodily regimens, constant fear of illness, or making preservation of life the chief aim are pernicious; moderation and a well-tempered mind are preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Valetudinarians' example (man weighing himself, timing sleep and meals, measuring perspiration) is given as folly: while reasonable care of health is prudent, converting all life into regimen and constant fear of death ruins enjoyment and can be self-destructive. 'Preservation of life should be only a secondary Concern, and the Direction of it our Principal.'
